title: Statistical Inference & Hypothesis Testing
summary: Confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, p-values, and Type I/II errors — the toolkit behind "is this difference real" questions.

slides.markdown:
The **population** is the entire group you actually care about (all users, all possible transactions); a **sample** is the subset you actually observed. **Point estimation** uses the sample to produce a single best-guess number for a population parameter — the sample mean estimates the population mean, for instance.

Every technique in this Topic exists because you almost never get to measure the whole population — inference is the machinery for making honest claims about the whole from a look at the part.

A **confidence interval** gives a range likely to contain the true population parameter, e.g. "95% CI for average session length: [4.2, 5.1] min."

**Wrong belief:** "there's a 95% chance the true mean falls in this specific interval." **Why it's wrong:** the true mean is a fixed (if unknown) number — either in the interval or not; no probability remains *after* it's computed. **Correct model:** 95% describes the *procedure* — repeat sampling-and-interval many times, about 95% of resulting intervals contain the true mean. The randomness is in the interval, not the fixed parameter.

Hypothesis testing starts by assuming a **null hypothesis** `H₀` ("no effect," "no difference") is true, and asks whether the observed data would be surprising under that assumption. If the data is surprising enough, you **reject** `H₀` in favor of the **alternative hypothesis** `H₁` (there is an effect).

Crucially, you never "prove `H₀` true" — failing to reject it just means the evidence wasn't strong enough to rule it out, which is a much weaker claim than "we've confirmed there's no effect."

A **p-value** is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as what you saw, **assuming `H₀` is true**. A small p-value (typically `<0.05`) is evidence against `H₀`.

**Wrong belief:** "the p-value is the probability H₀ is true" or "the result is due to chance." **Why it's wrong:** a p-value is computed by *assuming* `H₀` — it can't also state how likely `H₀` is. **Correct model:** p-value = `P(data this extreme | H₀ true)`, not `P(H₀ true | data)` — the same confusion as the prosecutor's fallacy in [bayes-theorem](bayes-theorem).

slides.sectionTitle: Type I vs Type II error
slides.markdown:
| | H₀ actually true | H₀ actually false |
|---|---|---|
| **Reject H₀** | Type I error (false positive), rate = `α` | Correct rejection |
| **Fail to reject H₀** | Correct | Type II error (false negative), rate = `β` |

![Type I and Type II error regions on overlapping null and alternative distributions](assets/type1-type2-error.svg)

The trade-off is fundamental: tightening the significance threshold `α` to catch fewer false positives raises the risk of missing real effects (higher `β`) — you can't shrink both simultaneously without more data.

assets.alt: Type I and Type II error regions on overlapping null and alternative distributions

slides.markdown:
**Statistical significance** (a small p-value) only tells you an effect is likely *real* (not due to chance) — it says nothing about whether the effect is **large enough to matter**. With a big enough sample size, even a genuinely trivial effect (a 0.001% conversion lift) can become statistically significant.

**Practical significance** asks the business question: is this effect size worth acting on? Always report both the p-value *and* the effect size with its own confidence interval — a significant-but-tiny effect might not justify the cost of shipping a change.

| | z-test | t-test |
|---|---|---|
| Population std. dev (`σ`) known? | Yes | No — estimated from the sample |
| Sample size | Works at any size (given known σ) | Better suited for small samples |
| Distribution used | Normal | Student's t (heavier tails, converges to Normal as sample size grows) |

In practice, `σ` is rarely known ahead of time, so the **t-test dominates real-world usage** — the t-distribution's heavier tails correctly account for the extra uncertainty of estimating `σ` from the same sample.

Running many hypothesis tests inflates the **overall** chance of a false positive, even if each individual test uses `α = 0.05`. Testing 20 independent, truly-null hypotheses at `α=0.05` gives roughly a `1 - 0.95²⁰ ≈ 64%` chance that **at least one** falsely appears significant, purely by chance.

**Corrections** like the **Bonferroni method** (divide `α` by the number of tests) control the overall false-positive rate, at the cost of reduced power to detect real effects — this is exactly why "we tested 50 metrics and found 3 significant ones" is a red flag, not a win, without correction.
